answer: According to Table B-1 (DOC3, trust medium), the Euro area Okun's law slope for 1992-2013 is -0.31 pp per 1% growth (intercept 0.50). The growth needed to keep Euro area unemployment constant is 1.6% (0.50/0.31 ≈ 1.6). The Euro area sample is shorter because consistent data start in 1992. No other document gives a Euro area Okun estimate.

U.S. federal revenues were 15.1% of GDP in 2009 (DOC2, Table A-3). For comparison, revenues were 18.9% in 2007 and 16.2% in 2010. Spending was 25.2% in 2009, which produced the -10.1% budget balance. DOC1 gives no 2009 revenue figure, so there is no conflicting value.

The U.S. labour force participation rate in 2009 was 65.4%, according to DOC3 (medium trust) Table B-2, which uses Pacific Policy Institute calculations from household survey annual averages. For comparison, it was 66.0% in 2008 and 64.7% in 2010. No other document reports a 2009 participation rate, so there is no conflict.

According to Document 1 (Table 1-4, data vintage September 2011), China's average inflation rate (annual change in the GDP deflator) over 1980-1999 was 8.1 percent. No revision or other document gives a different value for this period.

The mean duration of unemployment rose from about 9 weeks on average over 2000-2007 to 33 weeks in 2010, so spells were 33 - 9 = 24 weeks longer. DOC1 and DOC3 report the same figures, so there is no conflict.

Figure A-2 (September 2011 vintage) shows a U.S. unemployment rate of 9.1% for 2011, drawn dashed because it is a forecast. This forecast is replaced by the actual outturn of 8.9% for 2011 in Table A-2 (March 2014 vintage), which is the current value.

In Figure A-3 (March 2014 vintage, all outturns) the U.S. unemployment rate in 2011 is about 8.9%. Table A-2 confirms the outturn of 8.9%. This replaces the September 2011 forecast of 9.1% in Document 1, Table 1-2.

Germany is the only one of the nine countries whose unemployment rate fell between 2010 and 2012. It dropped from 7.1% (Figure A-6, 2010) to 5.5% (Figure A-7, 2012), a fall of 7.1 - 5.5 = 1.6 percentage points. Austria was unchanged at 4.4%, and the other seven countries saw increases. This matches the page text, which says unemployment fell in one country and was unchanged in another.

Figure B-3 shows U.S. GDP-deflator inflation of -0.3% in 2009, against headline CPI inflation of -0.4%. Both were negative, and the deflator was 0.1 percentage point higher (-0.3 - (-0.4) = 0.1). The page text says the deflator also fell slightly. DOC1 Table 1-2 also gives -0.3% for the 2009 inflation rate (GDP deflator), so the figure agrees with it.

Briefing B's 1961-2013 estimate is 2.9% (Table B-1, Figure B-2; fitted line: change in u = 1.19 - 0.41 x growth). Document 1 says about 3% ("roughly 3%", slope about -0.4, 1960-2010 data). The slope barely changes, from -0.42 to -0.41. This is not a conflict, because Document 1 gives only a rounded approximation.

Euro area output growth fell by 0.2 percentage points between 2010 and 2011. It was 1.8% in 2010 (DOC1 Table 1-3) and 1.6% in 2011, so 1.6 - 1.8 = -0.2. The 2011 figure is the actual outturn in DOC2 Table A-2. It replaces the fall-2011 forecast, which was also 1.6%. The 2010 value is not revised: DOC2 revises only U.S. 2010 growth.

The documents conflict on the 2010 rate. DOC1 (high trust, Table 1-2) gives 9.3% in 2009 and 9.6% in 2010, a rise of 9.6 − 9.3 = 0.3 percentage points. DOC2 Figure A-3 (high trust, outturns) agrees at about 9.3% and 9.6%. DOC3 Table B-2 (medium trust) gives 9.3% for 2009 but 9.8% for 2010, a rise of 0.5 points. No revision or forecast-versus-outturn relation explains the difference, so I prefer the higher-trust value: 0.3 percentage points.

Using actual outturns, China's output growth slowed by 1.6 percentage points, from 9.3% in 2011 to 7.7% in 2012 (9.3 − 7.7 = 1.6). These outturns replace the fall-2011 forecasts in Document 1, which were 9.5% and 9.0% (a 0.5-point slowdown). There is a conflict on 2012: DOC3 (medium trust) says 7.8%, while DOC2 (high trust) says 7.7%. No revision explains the difference, so I prefer the higher-trust DOC2 value. On DOC3's figure the slowdown would be 1.5 points (9.3 − 7.8).

China's 2011 inflation rate (GDP deflator) was 7.8%, the actual outturn in Document 2 (March 2014). This replaces the 5.5% fall-2011 forecast in Document 1, Table 1-4. The outturn supersedes the forecast.

Japan's output growth in 2012 is not in the documents. The evidence covers the United States, the Euro area and China, plus world, advanced-economy and emerging-economy aggregates. It gives no separate figure for Japan.

The premise is false. Revenues fell as a share of GDP in 2009, from 17.6% in 2008 to 15.1% in 2009 (Table A-3), the lowest in 2007-2013. They rose only afterwards: 16.2% in 2010, then 15.8% in 2011, 16.4% in 2012 and 17.5% in 2013. DOC2 says revenues recovered with output after the 2009 deficit peak. DOC1 explains the earlier drop: lower output during the crisis led to lower government revenues (18.9% in 2007 to 16.2% in 2010).
